name: Wallfahrtskloster Maria Waldrast
kurzbeschreibung: Maria Waldrast at 1,638 m at the foot of the Serles: Central Europe's highest monastery, a Servite pilgrimage site since 1407, and a legendary healing spring.
beschreibung:
Overview

The venerable Servite monastery Maria Waldrast is situated in a majestic high-alpine setting at 1,638 meters above sea level at the foot of the striking, 2,717-meter-high Serles („High Altar of Tyrol“) in the northern Wipptal. Located within the municipality of Mühlbachl near Matrei am Brenner, Maria Waldrast is regarded as the highest monastery in Central Europe and one of the oldest and most significant Marian sanctuaries in the entire Alpine region. Encircled by dense larch and stone pine forests, this time-honored pilgrimage destination unites deep spiritual contemplation, Baroque ecclesiastical art, and alpine mountain adventures against the sheer limestone cliffs of the Stubai Alps.

History & Healing Spring

The founding legend of Maria Waldrast dates back to 1392: two young shepherd boys, Hans and Christian Lusch from Mühlbachl, are said to have heard an angelic voice in a dream bidding them to enter the deep mountain forest. There, grown wondrously inside the trunk of a larch tree, they discovered a carved image of the Virgin Mary. In 1407, Prince-Bishop Ulrich von Wien of Brixen granted permission to build a chapel, which was solemnly consecrated on May 24, 1429. With the rapid growth of the pilgrim flock, sovereign Erzherzog Leopold V. endowed the construction of a monastery in 1621 for the mendicant order of the Serviten (Servants of Mary). Master builder Hans Alberthaler erected the Early Baroque pilgrimage church and convent building. Under Emperor Joseph II, the monastery was secularized in 1785 and fell temporarily into decline until the Servites returned in 1844 and lovingly restored the complex. The artistic highlight of the church is the Early Baroque high altar housing the Gothic miraculous image of the enthroned Muttergottes mit Kind (c. 1420). The Waldrast-Quelle enjoys international renown: the ice-cold mountain spring water emerges directly beneath the monastery from the limestone strata of the Serles; scientific analyses attest that the calcium- and sulfate-rich mineral water boasts exceptional purity, vitality, and geomantic power. Pilgrims and mountain hikers have collected the spring water from the carved wooden fountain for centuries.

Visit & Getting There

The pilgrimage church of Maria Waldrast is open daily year-round from approx. 07:00 to 19:00 with free admission. The adjoining traditional Klostergasthof offers pilgrims and day-trippers hearty Tyrolean cuisine as well as cozy overnight accommodations. Arriving by car: Via the Brennerautobahn A13 (exit Matrei am Brenner) or toll-free on the B182 to Matrei; from there, a well-maintained five-kilometer toll road ascends to the spacious car park directly at the monastery (toll approx. €6.00 per car). On foot or by cable car: A favorite route is riding the Serlesbahn gondola from Mieders in the Stubaital up to the Koppeneck mountain station (1,600 m), where a wonderful, virtually flat panoramic trail leads comfortably to Maria Waldrast in around 45 minutes. Alternatively, the historic pilgrim Way of the Cross climbs from Matrei in approximately 1.5 to 2 hours.

Tips

The monastery church, the inn, and the fountain courtyard are largely barrier-free and accessible with all-terrain strollers; the panoramic walking trail from the Serlesbahn summit station Koppeneck is wide, graveled, and well-suited for families. Bring empty water bottles along to fill up on fresh, energizing Waldrast spring water for your hike. In winter, an approximately five-kilometer natural toboggan run down to Matrei promises thrilling descents.
oeffnungszeiten: Wallfahrtskirche täglich 07:00–19:00 Uhr; Gasthof im Sommer täglich, im Winter Do–So
